Source: https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/weekly-recap-this2shell-that2shell.html
Context: https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/leaked-litellm-master-key-let-attackers.html
Context: https://forever.security/blog/hijacking-ai-agents-via-downloads-folder

The supplied article.txt is truncated at 681 bytes. The full source page was
recovered with curl and its body, links, images and code blocks extracted into
scratch/threat-feed/4309. There are no code blocks. The two downloaded images
are a recap illustration and a SANS advertisement, with no exploit bytes.
The full recap explicitly identifies malicious PyPI LiteLLM 1.107.0, describing
Python startup execution, credential harvesting and an hourly Unix backdoor.
It also names malicious npm function-color, with no version. PURLS preserves
that name alone; no version or source-package identity was invented.

Artifacts: forager fetch --all-wheels -o <scratch>/testdata
pkg:pypi/litellm@1.107.0 recovered seven platform wheels. Each wheel's METADATA
names litellm 1.107.0, and all hashes agree with Forager provenance. Wheels
reside in testdata/hostile; original .forage.json records remain separately in
downloads/pypi. Nothing was installed or executed. Analysis-only extracted
members and decoded source are outside the sample set.

The manylinux x86_64 wheel contains:
  litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/cook.pth: import cook
  litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/cook.py: Base64/zlib decoder and exec
  litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/sitecustomize.py: same credential collector,
    fork/setsid/dup2 daemon, requests response helper, compiled exec callback,
    and asyncio polling loop followed by time.sleep(3600).
The decoded collector constructs credential paths with separate arguments:
  os.path.join(PC_HOME, '.cargo', 'credentials.toml')
  os.path.join(PC_HOME, '.gem', 'credentials')
  os.path.join(PC_HOME, '.config', 'composer', 'auth.json')
  os.path.join(os.environ.get('APPDATA', ''), 'Composer', 'auth.json')
It reads these via pc_txt, collects additional browser/cloud/SSH/developer
secrets, serializes the results, encrypts with AES plus RSA-wrapped key, and
sends the packed body through urllib.request.Request(..., method='POST').
cleave facts on both original Python members recovered the decoded source.

Change: broaden the three canonical notable secret-config path observations
to recognize adjacent quoted path arguments, Windows native/escaped separators
and source-language scopes. Composer additionally accepts its Windows casing.
These are store references, not reads or theft. No severity was raised, no
family name, endpoint, payload filename or package identity gates detection.
Existing hostile rules already cover browser-password decryption, encrypted
developer/cloud secret export, HTTP code polling and Python startup persistence.
No duplicate hostile composite was added for those already detected outcomes.

False-positive correction: removed the unreferenced
objectives/execution/payload/script-eval::python-decrypted-payload-script-eval
composite. It combined a large Base64 literal, PBKDF2 and any exec/getattr at
archive scope, without a ciphertext-to-evaluator link or attacker-specific
admission. In these wheels, PBKDF2 decrypts browser passwords, whereas exec
runs zlib-decompressed source: there is no encrypted-code payload. Neither
plain getattr nor file-wide co-occurrence supports the claimed execution.
The neutral constituent observations remain, as do the independent hostile
credential, HTTP-polling and persistence detections. This is an intentional
detection correction, not a criticality demotion or a taxonomy relocation.

Consumer audit: Cargo and RubyGems marker IDs feed only neutral path/read
observations. The Composer ID also feeds the PHP credential-export composite,
which still requires HTTP POST and JSON serialization; a path reference alone
does not convict. The Ruby-specific gem-credentials-file literal observation
is unchanged. No directory move or reference rewrite was made.

Focused controls: /usr/local/var/cyclotron/cleave/tests/fixtures/trait-controls/threat-feed-4309
Run: python3 testdata/threat-feed-4309/check.py --fixtures <controls> --report <scratch>/controls.json
Twelve positives cover Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Ruby, Java, C#,
Rust, PHP and PowerShell, including Unix paths, Windows paths and path catalogs.
Four negatives cover different store files, wrong directory boundaries,
prose-only mentions, and unrelated PBKDF2/Base64/exec. Every control must
remain free of hostile findings.
All three updated observations also match the original decoded collector.

Indicator scope: the recap itself supplies no file hashes or malicious network
hosts. SHA256 records recovered wheel digests, not source commits. ENDPOINTS
records the directly linked LiteLLM account-compromise IP (69.48.229.143),
webhook.site credential-exfiltration service, and collector host litellm.dev
(www.litellm.dev in the recovered code). The shared service hostname does not
assert every tenant is malicious. The cited malicious webhook URLs are:
  https://webhook.site/65a42464-3cfa-4b02-a18c-17a6d7b86f37
  https://webhook.site/4da03473-a3e7-4dc2-a087-9c564b4208e1
The raw.githubusercontent.com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt
rendezvous in the sample is a specific URL; githubusercontent.com as a whole
is not an IOC. Public registries, research sites and fixed versions are excluded.

Limits: these edits address a demonstrated path-recognition gap in the
recovered LiteLLM artifacts. No new detections are claimed for the recap's
other exploit notices, Android RATs, Heartbreaker or agent-instruction payload.
Broader cross-function data-flow inference and arbitrary runtime string
construction remain beyond these path observations. A rule-load rejection
for noncapturing regex groups was corrected before any final sample analysis;
that invocation produced no reports and was not a sample-floor evaluation.

Focused verification: 16 fixture cases passed, with all three target path
observations at notable criticality and no hostile findings in any control.
The removed encrypted-payload claim is absent from the unrelated-crypto
regression control. Whitespace checks also passed.

Final atomscan verification: all seven original wheels pass the hostile
floor, each with 13 hostile and 9 suspicious findings. All three extended
notable path observations fire on each wheel. The unsupported encrypted-code
composite is absent. Counts are inherited archive findings, not a count of
distinct techniques; independently verified behaviors include browser password
decryption, encrypted credential export, HTTP code polling, and startup-hook
persistence. Full reports and per-wheel counts remain in scratch.
